title: NASA-UAP-D022, Gemini 9 Debriefing, 1966
what_is_it: A collection of internal NASA memoranda, routing slips, and telegraphic messages documenting the scientific experiments debriefing and status reporting for the Gemini IX-A mission in 1966.
core_summary: These documents record NASA's internal communications about the scientific experiments conducted during the Gemini IX-A mission (June 3-6, 1966), including airglow photography, micrometeorite collection, zodiacal light photography, and synoptic photography. The mission faced complications when the ATDA target vehicle's shroud failed to separate (dubbed 'an angry alligator' by astronaut Tom Stafford), preventing docking and the retrieval of the S-10 micrometeorite experiment. The EVA (spacewalk) proved too physically demanding for hand-held photography, and the Astronaut Maneuvering Unit exercise was unsuccessful.
interpretation_warnings: Despite the war.gov CSV description referencing astronaut accounts of 'flashing lights' and 'sparkles' on pages 2-5, the extracted text of this document contains no such accounts — the OCR may have failed to capture those pages or they may be in handwritten portions that were not legible to text extraction.
Much of the document consists of OCR-degraded text from handwritten routing slips and typed carbon copies, resulting in garbled or missing words throughout.

This is an administrative and scientific experiments status document, not a UAP investigation report; its inclusion in the PURSUE collection appears to relate to the unextracted 'flashing lights' observations mentioned in the CSV description.
The document is single-source (NASA internal communications from one office), reflecting the perspective of the Manned Flight Experiments Office rather than the astronauts directly.
Several handwritten routing slip annotations are largely illegible in the OCR output.

public_headline: NASA Internal Memos Detail Gemini 9 Science Experiments and Equipment Failures
public_tldr: This document is a collection of internal NASA memos and routing slips from 1966, recording the scientific experiments debriefing for the Gemini IX-A mission. It covers experiment results — including zodiacal light photography, airglow imaging, micrometeorite collection, and biological specimens — alongside equipment failures and the infamous 'angry alligator' docking target malfunction. It is an administrative record, not a UAP investigation report.
public_narrative:
In June 1966, NASA flew the Gemini IX-A mission with astronauts Thomas Stafford and Eugene Cernan in low Earth orbit over three days. This document, compiled primarily by J. R. Gill of NASA's Manned Flight Experiments Office, records the internal communications surrounding the mission's scientific experiments debriefing, held on 16 June 1966 at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston.

The mission carried several experiments but ran into significant problems. The Augmented Target Docking Adapter (ATDA) — the vehicle the crew was supposed to dock with — had a faulty shroud that failed to separate, making it impossible to dock or retrieve the S-10 micrometeorite collection experiment mounted on it. Stafford nicknamed the malfunctioning target 'an angry alligator' because of its appearance. The spacewalk proved so physically demanding that hand-held photography was deemed impractical, and the Astronaut Maneuvering Unit exercise failed because controlling body position required both hands, leaving none free for other tasks.

Despite the setbacks, several experiments produced useful results. The zodiacal light photographs, taken on Tri-X film, were judged the best yet obtained, surpassing those from Gemini V. About 40 usable airglow pictures were captured, and the micrometeorite collection surface recorded 9 impacts on the portion analysed. Over 300 colour photographs were taken with Hasselblad and Maurer cameras, and one image revealed a previously unmapped glacial lake in the Andes that posed a potential avalanche hazard to villages below — the Peruvian Embassy was informed and Peru sent a military plane to investigate. Biological experiments found that T-4 bacteriophages and penicillium specimens survived spaceflight, while two other specimens did not, and that areas inside the spacecraft that were contaminated before flight were found sterile afterward.

This document's inclusion in the war.gov PURSUE UAP release appears to relate to astronaut observations of 'flashing lights' and 'sparkles' referenced in the release's catalogue description. However, those specific accounts do not appear in the extracted text of the document — they may be in handwritten portions that could not be read by text extraction, or on pages the OCR process failed to capture. The document itself is administrative in nature, focused on experiment logistics and results rather than anomalous sightings.
